nameStory: The name 'scentless mayweed' tells you exactly what this plant isn't—it looks like mayweed but has no smell! True mayweed has a strong, unpleasant odor when crushed, but this lookalike is completely odorless. The 'May' part refers to when it typically starts blooming in its native Europe, though in New England it flowers throughout summer.
description: Scentless mayweed is a cheerful-looking annual wildflower that produces classic white daisy-like blooms with bright yellow centers. This European immigrant has made itself at home in New England's disturbed soils, growing 1-3 feet tall with finely divided, feathery leaves. It's a member of the huge sunflower family and looks almost exactly like chamomile or other mayweeds—except for one key difference you'll discover with your nose!

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White daisy-like flowers with 15-20 narrow petals surrounding a dome-shaped bright yellow center that's solid and buttonlike, about the size of your pinky nail

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Finely cut, feathery leaves that look almost lace-like, divided into thread-thin segments that feel soft and delicate between your fingers

idTips.label: Scent Test
idTips.description: Completely odorless when you crush the leaves or flowers—this is the key identifying feature that separates it from smelly mayweeds and chamomiles

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy annual plant growing 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems that spread outward, creating a somewhat sprawling appearance

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny brown seeds with three distinct ribs or ridges running lengthwise—this is where the scientific name 'Tripleurospermum' (three-ribbed seed) comes from

habitat: Look for scentless mayweed in disturbed soils like roadsides, agricultural field edges, vacant lots, and garden borders throughout New England. It thrives in sunny, open areas with poor to average soil and seems to particularly love recently disturbed ground. You'll often find it mixed with other weedy plants in areas where the soil has been turned over or compacted.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge with their characteristic feathery foliage, but flowers typically don't appear until late spring or early summer.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant white daisy flowers from June through August. This is the best time to practice your scent test for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by seed production. Plants begin to die back as temperatures drop since this is an annual.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain since this is an annual plant, but seeds lie dormant in the soil waiting for spring warmth.

funFact: This plant's scientific name 'Tripleurospermum' literally means 'three-ribbed seed'—and you can actually see these three tiny ridges on each seed with a magnifying glass, making it one of the few wildflowers you can identify by examining its seeds under magnification!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with German chamomile and other mayweeds, which look nearly identical. The foolproof test: crush some leaves and smell—scentless mayweed has absolutely no odor, while chamomile smells sweet and apple-like, and stinking mayweed smells terrible. Remember: 'No smell, scentless mayweed!'
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with the many other plants called 'chamomile'—true German chamomile is fragrant and used for tea, while scentless mayweed is odorless and not typically used medicinally. The word 'mayweed' itself comes from 'maiden weed,' referring to these delicate daisy-like flowers that often appear in fields.
compareHints: Since scentless mayweed is the only Tripleurospermum species commonly found in New England, compare it with its close relatives German chamomile and corn chamomile. German chamomile has a hollow flower center and sweet apple scent, while corn chamomile has a solid center like scentless mayweed but smells unpleasant. Scentless mayweed stands out as the only one that's completely odorless with a solid yellow center.
